Ludwig van Beethoven · 1770–1827 · Bonn · German composer and pianist

Ludwig van Beethoven (Bonn, 1770 – Vienna, 1827) was the composer who bridged the Viennese Classicism he inherited from Haydn and Mozart and the Romantic sensibility of the nineteenth century. His figure dominates the history of Western music: few composers who followed have escaped his influence, and few have been so widely admired by audiences and musicians alike.

💡 Mälzel's metronome
Beethoven was so taken with the metronome invented by Johann Mälzel that he wrote letters recommending it to publishers and began marking metronome tempos in his scores, so that his works would be played at the speed he had imagined. It is a telling detail for a musician who resisted taking orders from anyone.

Arturo Toscanini · 1867–1957 · Parma · Italian orchestra conductor

Arturo Toscanini (born Parma, 1867; died New York, 1957) was one of the most influential conductors in the history of Western music. The son of a tailor who had fought alongside Garibaldi, he showed an exceptional musical gift from childhood.

💡 A conductor at nineteen
In Rio de Janeiro, during a performance of Aida, the scheduled conductor quit hours before the show and the audience booed his replacement so fiercely that he could not even signal the orchestra. A young cellist in the pit climbed onto the podium, gave the cue and conducted the entire opera from memory. That moment launched his career.

Johann Sebastian Bach · 1685–1750 · Eisenach · German composer and organist

Johann Sebastian Bach (born Eisenach, 21 March 1685; died Leipzig, 28 July 1750) was a German composer and organist whose genius joined outstanding performing skill to a powerful and original creative imagination. As a keyboard virtuoso he acquired an almost legendary reputation in his lifetime, but it was as a composer that he secured a unique historical position by the end of the eighteenth century.

💡 Secret copying at night
After being orphaned, Bach went to live with his older brother in Ohrdruf. There he copied and studied music in secret, even though it was forbidden, since scores were precious and paper was expensive. The story goes that he spent long hours copying other masters' works by moonlight, revealing an early obsession with learning.

Franz Schubert · 1797–1828 · Vienna · Austrian composer

Franz Schubert (Vienna, 1797 – Vienna, 1828) was the only one of the great Viennese Classical composers to be born in the city itself, and his work decisively shaped orchestral music, chamber music, piano music and, above all, the German lied. His life, brief and apparently uneventful, has given rise to very different interpretations of both the man and his music, which remain hotly debated.

💡 A brother who couldn't keep up
His brother Ignaz tried to teach him piano, but the lessons lasted only a very short time: within a few months the boy had surpassed him. Later, his teacher Michael Holzer claimed he had nothing left to teach him, since the boy already knew everything he intended to pass on, and simply looked at him in amazement and silence.

Wilhelm Furtwängler · 1886–1954 · Berlin · German conductor, composer and writer

Wilhelm Furtwängler (born Berlin, 25 January 1886; died Baden-Baden, 30 November 1954) was a German conductor, composer and writer, widely regarded as one of the great interpreters of German music in the twentieth century.

💡 A puppet on a string
One of the musicians in his orchestra likened his podium movements to a marionette hanging from a string: awkward, ungainly gestures that seemed barely connected to the beat. Yet the players were captivated by his style, as if its very eccentricity was what held them spellbound.

Joseph Haydn · 1732–1809 · Rohrau · Austrian composer

Franz Joseph Haydn (Rohrau, Lower Austria, 1732 - Vienna, 1809) was the first of the three great Viennese Classics, alongside Mozart and Beethoven. His career spans the move from the traditional patronage system of the late Austrian Baroque to the figure of the independent artist that anticipates Romanticism.

💡 A head with its own journey
Shortly after Haydn was buried, phrenologists stole his head, eager to study the skull of a genius. The skull was not reunited with the rest of his remains until 1954, decades after his death.

Robert Schumann · 1810–1856 · Zwickau · German composer, pianist and music critic

Robert Schumann (Zwickau, 1810 – Endenich, near Bonn, 1856) was a German composer and, at the same time, one of the most influential music critics of his day. He is remembered above all for his piano music and his songs, but he cultivated nearly every genre of his time and also explored new ones.

💡 A hand that ended the dream of the piano
Schumann dreamed of becoming a great virtuoso, and his teacher promised he could be Europe's best pianist. A chronic problem in his right hand, whose causes sources describe differently, ended that career. He then poured his energy into composing.

Sir Henry J Wood · 1869–1944 · London · English conductor

Sir Henry J. Wood (born London, 3 March 1869; died Hitchin, 19 August 1944) was an English conductor, regarded as the first British-born career conductor and the founder of the promenade concerts that now bear his name. The son of an optician and engineering model-maker who was a keen amateur cellist and sang in the choir of St Sepulchres, Holborn, he was nurtured at home in his early musical aptitude.

💡 A great musical hoax
Tired of critics faulting every arrangement he made, Wood decided to play a joke on them. He presented his own orchestration of Bach's Toccata and Fugue in D minor as the work of an invented Russian composer, Paul Klenovsky. The press and the BBC praised its brilliant colour, and Wood kept the secret for five years before revealing it.

George Frideric Handel · 1685–1759 · Halle · German-born composer, active mainly in England

George Frideric Handel, born in Halle in 1685 and dying in London in 1759, was a German-born composer who became a naturalised Briton and is today regarded as one of the great masters of his age. For a long time his fame rested almost entirely on a handful of orchestral works and some oratorios, above all Messiah, yet his output spans virtually every musical genre of his time, both vocal and instrumental.

💡 The secret attic clavichord
According to his first biographer, John Mainwaring, Handel's father opposed any musical education and forbade instruments at home. The young boy reportedly hid a small clavichord in a room at the top of the house and slipped there to play while the family slept. Many scholars regard the tale as more romantic than documented.

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart · 1756–1791 · Salzburg · Austrian composer

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart (Salzburg, 1756 - Vienna, 1791) was an Austrian composer whose music synthesised many different strands: Italian opera, the instrumental traditions of Austria and southern Germany, and the idioms of his own day. Matured in Vienna from 1781 onwards, his style is regarded as a peak of Viennese Classicism.

💡 The emperor and the too many notes
After the premiere of The Abduction from the Seraglio, Emperor Joseph II remarked that the opera had too many notes. Mozart replied dryly by asking how many were needed. A short exchange that shows his bold character even when facing the most powerful people of his time.

Sir Thomas Beecham · 1879–1961 · St Helens · English conductor

Sir Thomas Beecham (born St Helens, Lancashire, 29 April 1879; died London, 8 March 1961) was an English conductor whose influence on British musical life in the first half of the twentieth century was profound.

💡 A conductor who mocked Hitler
During a tour of Germany with the London Philharmonic, Beecham gave a concert in Berlin attended by Adolf Hitler. He reportedly remarked audibly, without any discretion, that the old man was late. After that tour he turned down renewed invitations to perform in Germany.

Christoph Willibald, Ritter von Gluck · 1714–1787 · Erasbach · Bohemian-born composer of opera and ballet

Christoph Willibald Gluck, who later held the title Ritter von, was one of the most influential composers of the second half of the eighteenth century. He was born on 2 July 1714 at Erasbach, in the Upper Palatinate, and his family's line ran back to gamekeepers and servants of the Lobkowitz household in Bohemia, which helps explain his later links with that region.

💡 A family tale from his childhood
According to Gluck family tradition, his father rose to become gunbearer to Eugene of Savoy, the great imperial general. It is a story passed down within the family rather than a documented fact, yet it offers a glimpse of the forest-keeping world in which the composer grew up before his musical career began.

Hugo Wolf · 1860–1903 · Windischgraz · Austrian composer of lieder

Hugo Wolf (Windischgraz, Styria, 1860 - Vienna, 1903) was an Austrian composer whose most enduring achievement is the lied. Born in a small German-speaking town within a Slovene region, he belonged to the German cultural world of the Habsburg monarchy.

💡 Expelled from the conservatory
Wolf was dismissed from the Vienna Conservatory after two years for 'breach of discipline', although he claimed he had left out of frustration with the school's conservatism. His rebellious nature clashed with every institution he attended, and he was also thrown out of his first secondary school as 'wholly inadequate'.

Theodore Thomas · 1835–1905 · Esens · German-born American conductor

Theodore Thomas (Esens, East Frisia, 1835 – Chicago, 1905) was a German-born conductor who spent almost his entire career in the United States. His work was decisive in bringing European symphonic music to American audiences and in establishing the great city orchestras of the country.

💡 A legendary reply
In 1889, businessman Charles Norman Fay asked whether he would move to Chicago if given a permanent orchestra. The most repeated story says Thomas answered that he would go to hell if they gave him one. The quip reveals his weariness with temporary ensembles and the financial insecurity of constant touring.

Igor Stravinsky · 1882–1971 · Oranienbaum [now Lomonosov] · Russian composer, later naturalised French and American

Igor Fyodorovich Stravinsky was born in Oranienbaum, now Lomonosov, on the outskirts of St Petersburg, in 1882, and died in New York in April 1971. A Russian composer who acquired French nationality in 1934 and American nationality in 1945, he is one of the most performed and influential musicians of the twentieth century.

💡 The premiere scandal
The 1913 premiere of The Rite of Spring is remembered for a tumult so intense that, according to some accounts, fists flew among the audience and police had to keep watch during the second act. Reports of the exact scale of the uproar are debated and may be exaggerated, yet the story has become permanently attached to the work.

Franz Liszt · 1811–1886 · Raiding · Hungarian composer, pianist, conductor and teacher

Franz Liszt (Raiding, Hungary, 22 October 1811 – Bayreuth, 31 July 1886) was a Hungarian composer, pianist, conductor and teacher, and one of the central figures of Romanticism. He was the greatest piano virtuoso of his time, invented the symphonic poem, developed the technique of thematic transformation and pushed harmony towards territory that anticipates the 20th century.

💡 Lisztomania
On his tours of the 1840s Liszt's audiences bordered on hysteria: admirers fought over his gloves, his handkerchiefs and the broken strings of his piano, and some kept the stubs of his cigars. In 1844 the poet Heinrich Heine called the phenomenon "Lisztomania", a word now seen as a forerunner of pop-star fame.

Hans Freiherr von Bülow · 1830–1894 · Dresden · German conductor, pianist and composer

Hans Guido von Bülow was born in Dresden in 1830 and died in Cairo in 1894. A German conductor, pianist and composer, he had been trained for a legal career but devoted himself to music and became one of the most influential figures of the second half of the nineteenth century. His musical studies began at about the age of nine, with piano lessons from Friedrich Wieck.

💡 A conductor who demanded memory
Bülow required the musicians of the Meiningen orchestra to play all their parts from memory, an unusual discipline for his era. Among his lasting innovations was the pedal timpani, which today is a standard instrument in the symphony orchestra.

Benjamin Britten · 1913–1976 · Lowestoft · English composer, conductor and pianist

Benjamin Britten was born in a middle-class family on the Suffolk coast. His mother, Edith, a singer and pianist, was the emotional centre of his life and controlled it closely until her death in 1937. He was composing from a very early age, and before he was ten had written a remarkable number of pieces.

💡 Born on Saint Cecilia's Day
Britten came into the world on 22 November, the feast of Saint Cecilia, patron saint of music. Biographers often note the coincidence, which seems to fit a life devoted to composing. His mother, a talented amateur musician, gave him his first piano and notation lessons, while the rest of his family showed little interest in music.

Carl Maria von Weber · 1786–1826 · Eutin · German composer, conductor, pianist and music critic

Carl Maria von Weber (Eutin, 1786 – London, 1826) was a composer, conductor, pianist and critic, a prototypical nineteenth-century musician-critic who sought, through his works, his writings and his work as performer and conductor, to promote art and to educate an emerging middle-class audience.

💡 An acid that stole his voice
While a very young orchestra director in Breslau, he accidentally swallowed an acid used in printing workshops. The injury ruined his voice so badly that he could never sing again, a painful loss for someone who had sung capably since childhood.

Otto Klemperer · 1885–1973 · Breslau · German conductor and composer

Otto Klemperer (born Breslau, 14 May 1885 – died Zürich, 6 July 1973) was a German conductor and composer who ranks among the great interpreters of the symphonic and operatic repertoire of the twentieth century. His career, shaped by exile and an international reach, stretched from the Weimar Republic to his final concerts in London.

💡 A card from Mahler kept for life
Mahler wrote a short endorsement on a small card recommending Klemperer, and the conductor kept it for the rest of his days. On the strength of that simple note, he won his first post as chorus master and assistant conductor in Prague in 1907, showing how much a famous name could open doors.

Pyotr Il'yich Tchaikovsky · 1840–1893 · Kamsko-Votkinsk · Russian composer

Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky, born in 1840 in Kamsko-Votkinsk in Vyatka province, was the first composer of a new generation of fully professional Russians, one who could firmly absorb the symphonic traditions of Western Europe while imprinting them with a deeply personal and national character. He was the second son of Il'ya Petrovich Tchaikovsky, a mining engineer, and Aleksandra Andreyevna Assier.

💡 Lessons saved by a governess
By the age of six he was fluent in French and German, and his governess Fanny Dürbach kept much of his earliest work, including his first known compositions. She also became the source of several childhood stories that still help explain the boy who would later write for the whole world.

Josquin des Prez · 1450–1521 · nr Saint Quentin · French Renaissance composer

Josquin des Prez was, alongside Ockeghem, Du Fay, Palestrina, Lassus and Byrd, one of the great figures of the Renaissance. A French composer, his music bridges the sound-world of the late Middle Ages and that of the High Renaissance, and it served as a model for much of the sixteenth century. His name is a diminutive of Josse, a Breton saint active in northern France and Flanders in the seventh century, a name widespread in that region during the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

André Previn · b. 1929 · Berlin · American conductor, pianist and composer of German origin

André Previn (born Berlin, 6 April 1929) was a conductor, pianist and composer of German birth and American nationality, one of the most versatile figures in twentieth-century music. His career spanned film, jazz, symphonic music and popular television, and his work keeps the spirit of the complete musician in the eighteenth-century sense.

💡 The conductor who became a comedy sketch
Previn appeared as 'Mr Andrew Preview' in a 1971 Morecambe and Wise sketch. He conducted Grieg's piano concerto with Eric Morecambe as an inept soloist, after being tricked into the job with the promise that Yehudi Menuhin would play violin. When Morecambe accused him of playing all the wrong notes, the comedian retorted that he had played all the right notes, just not in the right order. Years later, Previn said British taxi drivers still greeted him by that name.

Giuseppe Verdi · 1813–1901 · Roncole · Italian opera composer

Giuseppe Verdi (1813-1901) is, by almost common consent, the greatest Italian musical dramatist of the nineteenth century. Born at Roncole, near Busseto, in the Duchy of Parma, his reputation went far beyond opera, and he came to stand for the emerging Italian nation itself.

💡 A pushing father
The childhood story Verdi dictated late in life is now questioned. Historians believe his ambitious father, an innkeeper, drove his education firmly, while the composer liked to present himself as a peasant boy with little schooling. His early precocity was, according to these studies, the result of a sustained and sophisticated formal training.

Hector Berlioz · 1803–1869 · La Côte-Saint-André · French composer, critic and conductor

Hector Berlioz was born in La Côte-Saint-André in the département of Isère, into a comfortable family with deep roots in the region. His father, Louis-Joseph Berlioz, a respected physician of liberal outlook, was his first intellectual mentor; his mother, sterner and more devout, offered a sharp contrast. The grandeur of the Isère plain, with the Alps rising in the distance, left a lasting mark on the young boy.

💡 A revenge plan abandoned on the road
After Marie Moke broke off their engagement, Berlioz set out from Rome with a disguise, poisons and pistols to kill her, her mother and her new fiancé, and then himself. He got as far as Nice before he gave up the scheme and returned to Italy. It is one of the most dramatic episodes of his youth, and it shows how violent his romantic despair could become.

John Blow was one of the foremost English musicians of the second half of the seventeenth century, a central figure of the Restoration school and the teacher of a whole generation of composers. Blow wrote the so-called club anthem I will always give thanks while still a young chorister, together with Pelham Humfrey and William Turner. It may have honoured a victory over the Dutch, or more probably just marked the friendship of the three boys who sang together.

John Cage was born in Los Angeles on 5 September 1912 and died in New York on 12 August 1992. After a couple of lessons, Arnold Schoenberg told Cage he lacked any aptitude for harmony and would run into a wall he could never break through. His music, with more dissonance and attention to anger and jealousy, foreshadowed Weber and Berlioz.
